titre: The 1940 Law Promised a Ratification That Was Never Held
accroche: The constitutional law of July 10, 1940 charges Pétain with writing a constitution that “will be ratified by the Nation.” It never was.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 10, 1940, in Vichy, the National Assembly, that is, the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate meeting together, votes a constitutional law of a single article. Eighty parliamentarians vote against. The text is promulgated the same day by the President of the Republic, Albert Lebrun, and countersigned by the President of the Council, Marshal Pétain. It appears in the Journal officiel of July 11.

## What the single article says

The National Assembly “gives all powers to the Government of the Republic, under the authority and signature of Marshal Pétain, for the purpose of promulgating by one or several acts a new constitution of the French State.” This constitution “must guarantee the rights of labor, family, and fatherland.” And above all: “It will be ratified by the Nation and applied by the Assemblies it will have created.”

The delegation is therefore conditional. It grants the power to write a constitution, not the power to govern without one, and it provides for a final act that does not belong to the government: ratification by the Nation.

## What became of the condition

The text does not suspend the constitutional laws of 1875. Pétain nevertheless interprets it that way: the very next day, by Constitutional Act No. 2, he sets the powers of the head of the French State. Between 1940 and 1942, he gradually establishes his regime through a dozen constitutional acts.

The promised constitution is never promulgated. The regime has a draft written, which today's National Assembly describes as drawn up outside any democratic procedure: a head of state titled “President of the Republic,” elected for ten years by a National Congress, and a Chamber of Deputies elected by direct universal suffrage. A draft constitution, signed by Pétain on January 30, 1944, is published, but it is never submitted to the ratification that the 1940 law required.

## What this changes

On August 9, 1944, the Provisional Government of the French Republic does not merely repeal. Its ordinance proclaims in Article 1: “The form of the Government of France is and remains the Republic. In law it has never ceased to exist.” Article 3 “expressly” declares null the “act known as the ‘constitutional law of July 10, 1940’” and “all the acts known as ‘constitutional acts.’”

The difference between repealing and declaring null is considerable. A repeal leaves the past standing: the act existed, and it ceases to have effect. Nullity says that, in law, it was never valid. Yet it does not erase everything at once: Article 7 of the same ordinance lets the acts of the de facto authority whose nullity is not expressly declared continue to apply provisionally. For four years, a power exercised on a provisional basis rested on a law that promised a ratification no one ever organized.

Can a delegation written with its own condition last four years without the condition being met, and at what point does a provisional power stop being provisional?

repere.texte: The single article of the French constitutional law of July 10, 1940 charges the government, under Pétain's authority, with promulgating a new constitution, which “will be ratified by the Nation and applied by the Assemblies it will have created.” The ordinance of August 9, 1944 declares this law and all the “constitutional acts” null.
repere.source: Journal officiel de la République française, no. 167, July 11, 1940; ordinance of August 9, 1944, Article 3

carte.punch: July 10, 1940: a constitution that “will be ratified by the Nation.” It never was.
carte.idee: The French constitutional law of July 10, 1940 gives the Pétain government all powers to write a constitution, which “will be ratified by the Nation.” It never is. In 1944, an ordinance declares this law null, not merely repealed.
carte.source_courte: JO of July 11, 1940; ordinance of August 9, 1944

quiz.question: According to the July 10, 1940 law itself, why could the Vichy constitution never become a regular constitution?
choix: Because the law limited full powers to six months, a deadline passed by January 1941
Because the condition set by the law, ratification by the Nation, was never fulfilled
Because the law reserved promulgation to President Lebrun, who refused to sign
Because the Senate had refused to vote for the law, which only the Chamber had adopted
quiz.explication: The single article says the constitution “will be ratified by the Nation”: this condition was never organized. The law sets no six-month deadline, Lebrun promulgated it, and the vote took place before the National Assembly, Chamber and Senate meeting together.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many parliamentarians vote against the constitutional law of July 10, 1940?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that eighty parliamentarians vote against the law of July 10, 1940, before the National Assembly bringing together the Chamber and the Senate.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Pétain do the day after the vote, on July 11, 1940?
choix: He publishes Constitutional Act No. 2 on the powers of the head of state
He immediately submits his draft constitution to ratification by the Nation
He calls new legislative elections to renew the Chamber
He resigns as President of the Council in favor of President Lebrun
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The day after the vote, by Constitutional Act No. 2, Pétain sets the powers of the head of the French State, without waiting for the promised ratification.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What difference does the ordinance of August 9, 1944 establish by declaring the 1940 law null rather than repealed?
choix: None, the two words are synonymous in this text
Repeal erases all past effects, while nullity erases none
Nullity applies only to the Senate, while repeal would have targeted the whole National Assembly
Nullity says the act was never valid in law, whereas a repeal leaves the past standing
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text contrasts nullity and repeal: nullity means the act was never valid in law, while repeal leaves standing what existed before it.
